name: Strategy
intent: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms and let the caller swap them at runtime.
scenario: A checkout computes the price after a discount. Regular price, 20% off and $15 off are all different rules for the same job.
problem: Checkout has to apply different discount rules. Putting them all in one method with if/else makes the method grow with every promotion, and the rule is picked by a string instead of being an object you can swap and test.
solution: Pull each rule into its own object behind one small interface, apply(total). Checkout holds a reference to the current strategy and calls it. Swapping the rule is just assigning a different object.
pain: Checkout.total() has one branch per discount type
Every new promotion edits the same method
The rule is chosen by a string like "percent"
You cannot test one discount without running all the others' code
benefits: A new promotion is a new class or function, no edits to Checkout
The rule can be swapped while the program runs
Each rule can be tested on its own
whenToUse: You have several ways to do the same job and want to choose at runtime
A class has a big if/else or switch that selects between algorithms
You want to isolate rules so they can be tested and reused separately
whenNotToUse: There are only two stable options: a simple parameter or if may be clearer
The algorithms never change at runtime and share lots of state with the host class
Callers would need to understand every strategy to pick one well
pitfalls: Class count grows: in many languages a plain function or lambda is enough
Strategies that need lots of context from the host class leak its internals
Clients must know the strategies exist to choose one, so selection logic moves rather than disappears
Easy to confuse with State, which swaps behaviour automatically as an object changes

roles.label: Context
roles.description: Holds a strategy and delegates the work to it.

quiz.question: A checkout total() method branches on a discount string such as percent or flat. Marketing launches a new promotion every week, and last week the typo "percnt" silently gave no discount. What is the best refactoring?
options: Put each rule behind a Discount interface and let checkout call the chosen object
Add a constant for each discount name and keep the if/else branches inside total(), so typos become compile errors
Move the branches into a helper method that returns the new total
Pass the discount as a number and let total() subtract it
quiz.explanation: Each rule becomes an object, so a new promotion is a new class and a mistyped name can no longer silently pick nothing. Constants and a helper method still keep every rule in one growing branch. A plain number cannot express rules like "20 percent off".

quiz.question: In a scripting language, a list view must sort by price, by name or by rating, chosen by the user at runtime. Each ordering is two lines of code. The team debates writing a SortStrategy interface with three classes. What is the best advice?
options: Pass a plain comparison function, because a function is already a strategy
Create the three classes, because without a SortStrategy interface and concrete classes this is not a real strategy
Use a template method with a base class and three subclasses instead
Use one sort function with a switch on a sort key and no objects
quiz.explanation: The pattern is the interchangeable algorithm, not the classes, and a function value does that job with less code. Requiring classes confuses the form with the idea. A switch brings back the branching that grows with each new ordering.

quiz.question: After moving discount rules into strategy objects, a controller now holds a 40 line if/else over customer tier, coupon and region to pick which strategy to build. A reviewer says the mess has just moved. What is the best next step?
options: Let each strategy check the order and switch to the next one itself, as states do
Move the selection into one factory or rule table with its own tests
Fold the strategies back into checkout, since the choice logic needs them there
Apply every strategy and keep the best total
quiz.explanation: Selection logic does not vanish with Strategy, so it should live in one place that is easy to test. Folding back loses isolation. Strategies swapping themselves is State, and applying every strategy changes the business rule to best-of-all.
